title: Cisco Talos discloses first autonomous AI command-and-control malware, releases CAIRN hunting toolkit
subtitle: CLOSEDQUORUM is a Windows implant that delegates its next-move decisions to a voting panel of four commercial LLMs — DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, and Google Gemini — instead of a human operator, and Talos open-sourced a research toolkit for the emerging class.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: On September 22, 2026, Cisco Talos published research on CLOSEDQUORUM, which it describes as the first publicly documented Windows implant to delegate tactical command-and-control decisions to a panel of commercial large language models. Instead of contacting a dedicated attacker-operated server, the 16.4-megabyte Go binary calls four LLM APIs — DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, and Google Gemini — and lets a majority vote across their responses select its next action. Talos linked binary artifacts to postings on carding forums dating back to 2025 and released CAIRN, the Cognitive Artifact Intelligence Research Network, an open-source toolkit for hunting AI-integrated malware.

The significance is architectural, not just capability-driven. Traditional C2 traffic can be blocked by taking down a known-bad domain or IP. CLOSEDQUORUM's traffic looks like ordinary calls to four widely-used LLM APIs — traffic that most enterprise environments cannot block without breaking legitimate applications. And because the model panel picks the next step, the operator does not need to be online. Talos concluded that autonomous LLM-based C2 decision-making significantly reduces the need for manual operator effort, allowing an attack to run unattended and uninterrupted indefinitely.

This is the second time in six weeks that a novel LLM-abuse pattern has moved from research demo to attributed malware. In early July, the Jadepuffer agentic ransomware disclosed by Sysdig was the first commodity family to embed an LLM planner. CLOSEDQUORUM extends the pattern to voting across independent providers, which raises the bar on both detection — no single provider sees the whole attack — and takedown — any three providers can carry the load. Providers now face a policy question about whether their terms of service and abuse tooling need to change specifically for programmatic, multi-provider call patterns that no legitimate application uses.

Takeaway for learners — this is a case study in how the attack surface for AI systems is expanding beyond jailbreaking a model. The models here are not being jailbroken. They are being called with mundane-looking prompts as part of a distributed decision engine. Defenders who only think about model safety miss the API-abuse layer, and providers who only think about terms of service miss the traffic-pattern layer. If you are building anything that uses several model providers in parallel, expect API-level anomaly detection to become a real product category over the next year.
